g.text: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success in a variety
of tasks, ranging from machine translation to conversational AI.
g.title: N1 [Context] (cites=0) Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success in a variety of tasks, ranging from machine translation to conversational AI.

g.text: LLM training needs huge compute + memory
However, pretraining and fine-tuning LLMs with billions of parameters
requires a large amount of compute and GPU memory, not only to store the
parameters but also to compute gradients and optimizer states (e.g.,
g.title: N2 [Context] (cites=0) However, pretraining and fine-tuning LLMs with billions of parameters requires a large amount of compute and GPU memory, not only to store the parameters but also to compute gradients and optimizer states (e.g., momentum and historical gradients in Adam).

g.text: For example, full finetuning a relatively small LLM, such as Phi-2 with 2.7B
parameters, using a batch size of 128 requires at least 44 GB of GPU memory.
g.title: N3 [Context] (cites=0) For example, full finetuning a relatively small LLM, such as Phi-2 with 2.7B parameters, using a batch size of 128 requires at least 44 GB of GPU memory.

g.text: The large memory requirement makes it prohibitive to train such models with
larger batch sizes, which effectively improves the convergence and can
g.title: N4 [Context] (cites=0) The large memory requirement makes it prohibitive to train such models with larger batch sizes, which effectively improves the convergence and can improve performance.

g.text: Question: small batches with large-batch benefits?
This raises a key question: can we train LLMs with smaller mini-batches and
get the benefits of training with larger batch sizes?
g.title: N5 [Context] (cites=0) This raises a key question: can we train LLMs with smaller mini-batches and get the benefits of training with larger batch sizes?

g.text: To address this problem, many memory-efficient techniques have
been recently proposed, mainly to enable efficient fine-tuning of
g.title: N6 [Prior_Work] (cites=0) To address this problem, many memory-efficient techniques have been recently proposed, mainly to enable efficient fine-tuning of pretrained language models.

g.text: At a high level, such methods aim to find a smaller set of
parameters (Adelman et al., 2021), or find low-rank (Hu et al.,
2021; Zhao et al., 2024b) or quantized (Dettmers et al., 2022)
weights or optimizer states to train the model in a…
g.title: N7 [Prior_Work] (cites=4) At a high level, such methods aim to find a smaller set of parameters (Adelman et al., 2021), or find low-rank (Hu et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2024b) or quantized (Dettmers et al., 2022) weights or optimizer states to train the model in a memory-efficient manner.

g.text: There have also been efforts to adapt gradient-free optimization for
g.title: N8 [Prior_Work] (cites=1) There have also been efforts to adapt gradient-free optimization for training LLMs (Malladi et al., 2023).

g.text: Yet, most memory-efficient techniques cannot achieve a comparable
performance to training the full model parameters, or considerably
g.title: N9 [Limitation] (cites=0) Yet, most memory-efficient techniques cannot achieve a comparable performance to training the full model parameters, or considerably increase the training time.

g.text: In this work, we address the above problem from the data
g.title: N10 [Method] (cites=0) In this work, we address the above problem from the data perspective.

g.text: Specifically, we target finding smaller mini-batches of examples that
simulate or outperform training with larger mini-batches.
g.title: N11 [Method] (cites=0) Specifically, we target finding smaller mini-batches of examples that simulate or outperform training with larger mini-batches.

g.text: If this can be done, it directly improves the convergence rate of training
or fine-tuning with mini-batch stochastic gradient methods, and can yield
g.title: N12 [Method] (cites=0) If this can be done, it directly improves the convergence rate of training or fine-tuning with mini-batch stochastic gradient methods, and can yield superior performance.

g.text: To achieve this, an effective approach is to find smaller
mini-batches that closely capture the gradient of large random
g.title: N13 [Prior_Work] (cites=1) To achieve this, an effective approach is to find smaller mini-batches that closely capture the gradient of large random batches (Yang et al., 2023).

g.text: Smaller mini-batches (coresets) selected by this approach are
medoids (centroids) of the data in gradient space, weighted by
their corresponding cluster size (Mirzasoleiman et al., 2020).
g.title: N14 [Prior_Work] (cites=1) Smaller mini-batches (coresets) selected by this approach are medoids (centroids) of the data in gradient space, weighted by their corresponding cluster size (Mirzasoleiman et al., 2020).

g.text: Despite its promise on classification tasks, this approach is
infeasible and ineffective for pre-training or fine-tuning LLMs,
g.title: N15 [Limitation] (cites=0) Despite its promise on classification tasks, this approach is infeasible and ineffective for pre-training or fine-tuning LLMs, as we discuss below.

g.text: Firstly, language data is often a mixture of highly imbalanced sources (e.g.
categories or types of instructions). In this case, we show that smaller
mini-batch coresets do not contain representative examples from the small
g.title: N16 [Limitation] (cites=0) Firstly, language data is often a mixture of highly imbalanced sources (e.g. categories or types of instructions). In this case, we show that smaller mini-batch coresets do not contain representative examples from the small sources, and obtain poor performance.

g.text: Secondly, Adam is the standard optimizer for training LLMs, and small
mini-batches that capture the vanilla gradient of larger batches are not
g.title: N17 [Limitation] (cites=0) Secondly, Adam is the standard optimizer for training LLMs, and small mini-batches that capture the vanilla gradient of larger batches are not optimal for training with Adam.

g.text: Finally, the very large dimensionality of the LLM gradients makes pairwise
distances vacuous and the medoids cannot be found accurately.
g.title: N18 [Limitation] (cites=0) Finally, the very large dimensionality of the LLM gradients makes pairwise distances vacuous and the medoids cannot be found accurately.

g.text: These challenges make finding mini-batch coresets for training LLMs
inherently much more challenging to address.
g.title: N19 [Limitation] (cites=0) These challenges make finding mini-batch coresets for training LLMs inherently much more challenging to address.

g.text: In this work,we propose Coresets for Training LLMs(CoLM) by making
g.title: N20 [Method] (cites=0) In this work,we propose Coresets for Training LLMs(CoLM) by making the following contributions:

g.text: First, we show that w.h.p. mini-batch
coresets only contain medoids of the big
sources with a large-enough number of
g.title: N21 [Contribution] (cites=0) First, we show that w.h.p. mini-batch coresets only contain medoids of the big sources with a large-enough number of samples.
N21b [Contribution] (cites=0) Thus, examples selected via gradient matching from small sources are not representative and do not benefit learning other examples in their sources.
N21c [Contribution] (cites=0) Therefore, it is crucial to include all examples of the small sources in the mini-batch coresets.
N21d [Contribution] (cites=0) Besides, to enhance learning small sources, we weight all examples in the mini-batch coresets uniformly.

g.text: Next, to find mini-batch coresets for
training with Adam, we normalize gradients
where the historical terms are only…
g.title: N22 [Contribution] (cites=0) Next, to find mini-batch coresets for training with Adam, we normalize gradients by their historical exponential average, where the historical terms are only calculated for examples in the big sources.
N22b [Contribution] (cites=0) We find medoids of the big sources based on their normalized gradients.

g.text: Finally, to enable finding medoids in the
use zeroth-order methods to find smooth
gradient of the last V -projection matrix…
g.title: N23 [Contribution] (cites=0) Finally, to enable finding medoids in the very high-dimensional gradient space, we use zeroth-order methods to find smooth gradient of the last V -projection matrix in a memory-efficient way, and sparsify it via a source-wise mask, which keeps dimensions with the largest normalized gradient magnitude.
N23b [Contribution] (cites=0) We use ℓ1 distance between sparse gradients to find medoids of big sources.

g.text: We evaluate CoLM on the challenging task of
g.title: N24 [Contribution] (cites=4) We evaluate CoLM on the challenging task of mathematical problem-solving, by fine-tuning Phi-2, Phi-3 (Li et al., 2023b), Zephyr (Tunstall et al., 2023), and Llama-3 models (Dubey et al., 2024) using LoRA on the MathInstruct dataset (Yue et al., 2023) containing 14 highly imbalanced sources.
N24b [Contribution] (cites=1) Additionally, we apply CoLM to datasets in SuperGLUE benchmark (Wang et al., 2019), where we find sources by clustering the model's hidden states during the training.
N24c [Contribution] (cites=0) Remarkably, CoLM reduces the memory requirement of fine-tuning by 2x and even outperforms training with 4x larger random mini-batches.
N24d [Contribution] (cites=0) Compare to mini-batch of the same size, CoLM outperforms by up to 7.1% and 20% on several in- and out-domain tasks.

g.text: Notably, our approach can be easily stacked
training methods to further reduce the
memory requirements of training LLMs, as we…
g.title: N25 [Contribution] (cites=0) Notably, our approach can be easily stacked with LoRA, and other memory-efficient training methods to further reduce the memory requirements of training LLMs, as we confirm in our experiments.
